steps.user_message: I want to file my 2023 taxes correctly. I'm married filing jointly in Chicago IL. W-2 from Riverside Hospital: $79,400. Additional income: $22,100 (IT contracting, 2 clients), $1,780 from Discover Bank savings, $290 from Interactive Brokers. Home office: 155 sq ft exclusive; I pay $1,720/month for 750 sq ft. Deductions: $4,100 student loan interest (FedLoan, 2018–2019); $800 to Northwest Harvest (food bank) have the receipt; $950 unreimbursed expenses. Can you tell me what I can deduct, whether to itemize or take the standard deduction, how to treat the home office, and what forms I need?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Short answer up front
- Treat your IT contracting as self‑employment (Schedule C). That lets you deduct the home‑office (regular method looks better than the simplified method here) and business expenses against the $22,100.
- You can only deduct up to $2,500 of student‑loan interest (not the full $4,100) and it’s an above‑the‑line adjustment (Schedule 1) if your MAGI is below the phaseout range.
- With the numbers you gave (I assume your spouse had no other income), the standard deduction for Married Filing Jointly ($27,700 for 2023) is almost certainly better than itemizing (your itemizable deductions are small). So you’ll most likely take the standard deduction.
- Key federal forms you’ll need: Form 1040, Schedule 1 (adjustments including student‑loan interest / half SE tax), Schedule C (self‑employment business income/expenses), Schedule SE (self‑employment tax), Form 8829 (if you use the regular home‑office method), and Schedule B (because total interest > $1,500). Possibly Schedule A only if you choose to itemize.

Detailed walk‑through and calculations
Assumptions: I used only the income/amounts you provided and assumed your spouse had no other income. If your spouse has income, some results (student loan phaseout, itemizing decision) could change — see questions at the end.

1) How to treat each income item
- W‑2 from Riverside Hospital ($79,400) — reported as wages on Form 1040.
- IT contracting ($22,100 with 2 clients) — treated as self‑employment income (Schedule C). Report gross receipts, subtract business expenses on Schedule C to get net profit.
- Interest: Discover savings $1,780 and Interactive Brokers $290 = total interest $2,070. Because total interest > $1,500, you should complete Schedule B and include the interest on Form 1040.

2) Business expenses and the $950
- If the $950 are expenses related to your contracting work (tools, software, travel, phone, etc.), they are deductible on Schedule C. If they are unreimbursed employee expenses for Riverside Hospital employment, they are not deductible for 2018–2025 (suspended by TCJA).
- Clarify whether the $950 are contractor (business) expenses or unreimbursed employee expenses.

3) Home‑office deduction (you: renter)
- Your home office meets the square‑foot test: 155 sq ft exclusive use out of 750 sq ft total = 155/750 = 20.6667% of the home.
- Annual rent = $1,720 × 12 = $20,640.
- Regular method (recommended here): deductible rent portion = $20,640 × 20.6667% ≈ $4,266.67. You can also allocate utilities, renter’s insurance, etc., in the same percentage if you have those bills.
- Simplified method: $5 × 155 sq ft = $775.
- Because $4,266.67 (regular) > $775 (simplified), the regular method likely gives a larger deduction. If you use the regular method you generally file Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home) and report the result on Schedule C.
- Important: home office deduction is only available for self‑employed (Schedule C). Employees generally cannot claim it.

4) Student loan interest
- Student loan interest is an above‑the‑line adjustment up to $2,500 (not $4,100). The $4,100 you paid is more than the allowed maximum; you can only claim up to $2,500, subject to MAGI phaseouts.
- Phaseout: the deduction phases out based on your modified AGI (MAGI). Given the income items you listed (assuming spouse has no other income), your MAGI will be well under the MFJ phaseout threshold, so you are likely eligible for the full $2,500, but confirm if your spouse has other income or large items that raise MAGI.

5) Self‑employment tax and the half‑SE tax deduction
- Your contracting net income (after Schedule C expenses and home office) will be subject to self‑employment tax (Social Security/Medicare). You pay SE tax via Schedule SE (≈15.3% on 92.35% of net SE earnings).
- Half of the SE tax is deductible as an adjustment to income on Schedule 1 (reduces your AGI).

6) Quick illustrative calculation (using your numbers; assumes the $950 are business expenses and spouse has no other income)
- Contracting gross: 22,100
- Subtract business expenses: 950
- Subtract home‑office (regular method, rent portion): 4,266.67
=> Net self‑employment profit ≈ 16,883.33

- Self‑employment tax ≈ 16,883.33 × 0.9235 × 0.153 ≈ $2,386 (approx)
- Half SE tax deductible ≈ $1,193

- Total income before adjustments = W‑2 79,400 + interest 2,070 + net SE 16,883.33 = 98,353.33
- Subtract above‑the‑line items: half SE tax ≈ 1,193 and student loan interest (max) 2,500
=> AGI ≈ 94,660

- Standard deduction MFJ (2023): 27,700
=> Taxable income ≈ 94,660 − 27,700 = 66,960

Note: these are approximate computations to show how the pieces interact. Your exact tax will vary with exact figures, any spouse income, other deductions/credits, and rounding.

7) Itemize vs. standard deduction
- Your only listed potential itemized deduction is $800 charitable giving (Northwest Harvest). You did not list mortgage interest, property tax, large state income tax, or large medical expenses. With only $800 in known itemizable amounts, itemizing is far below the MFJ standard deduction of $27,700 — so take the standard deduction in almost all scenarios based on the numbers you gave.
- If you have sizable state/local taxes or mortgage interest you didn’t list, re‑check — but otherwise standard deduction is the choice.

8) Forms you will likely prepare/need
- Form 1040 (federal individual return)
- Schedule 1 (adjustments to income — e.g., student loan interest, half SE tax)
- Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business) for the contracting income
- Schedule SE (self‑employment tax)
- Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home) if you use the regular method for the home office; not needed if you use the simplified method
- Schedule B (interest and ordinary dividends) since total interest > $1,500
- Schedule A only if you decide to itemize (not likely here)
- Ensure you have Form 1098‑E (student loan interest statement), any 1099‑NEC/1099‑MISC from clients, 1099‑INT, and your W‑2

9) Records to keep / documentation
- FedLoan 1098‑E or statement showing interest paid (you have that).
- Charity receipt for Northwest Harvest (you said you have it) — keep the receipt.
- Rent receipts/lease, utility bills, floorplan or documentation showing square footage for home office, and records showing exclusive use of that space.
- Receipts for the $950 business expenses and any other contractor expenses.
- Records of any 1099s you received.

10) Other notes and recommendations
- If the $950 are employee unreimbursed expenses, they are not deductible for 2018–2025.
- If your contracting income is small and the home‑office deduction creates a loss, be aware of passive activity or hobby rules — but ordinary business losses from self‑employment generally offset other income unless special rules apply. If the loss is large or creates unusual tax attributes, consult a tax pro.
- You will owe self‑employment tax on net SE profit. For future years, consider quarterly estimated tax payments to avoid penalties.
- State (Illinois) return: you also need to file IL‑1040 and follow Illinois rules; the home‑office deduction and student loan adjustments may differ on the state return.

Questions for you / next steps I can help with
1. Are the $950 unreimbursed expenses related to your contracting work (i.e., business expenses)? Or are they unreimbursed employee expenses from Riverside Hospital?
2. Does your spouse have any income or deductions I should include? (That impacts MAGI, student loan phaseouts, and the itemize/standard decision.)
3. Do you want me to prepare a more precise worksheet with the exact numbers (rounded to cents) or draft an email to a tax preparer with these facts and ask for their help?

If you confirm the answers to Q1 and Q2, I’ll run a tighter line‑by‑line estimate and list any additional forms you may need for Illinois.
